chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
title: Union scale and pay in the dance school
summary: The dancing schools drew few name musicians; McRae says fifty dollars a week was good money, with union scale around fifty-five at Chick Webb's.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Some of these musicians you're talking about at the -- when the stock market fell and these, say, dime dances and so forth, who were some of the big name musicians who did come in there to play?
Did --
Oh, they would drop by -- by the Rhythm Club?
Well no, not the Rhythm Club, but the place on 14th Street.
We didn't have too many musicians coming in those places. Because, see, this

was a thing where you're really working. When you go to work. You're paid and people -- you know, you got to prove -- you got a house full of people there. All these men come out to the place -- the weekend be packed, you know, Friday and Saturday. (Inaudible) packed.
You were playing -- you were a member of the union at that time?
Oh yeah, sure.
So you were getting paid the scale. What was the scale of a union musician, say, in 1929?
Very low. Say if you were making fifty dollars a week, you were making a lot of money.
Just for --
That was top money if you got that kind of money in dance school. That was a lot of money.

Fifty dollars a week.

You know, one of the books I did for Life & Time, I think I showed you an article that -- we always, like (inaudible) the whole time we was with Chick, the union scale up there was around about fifty-five dollars. That was considered big money.
Fifty-five a week.

Fifty-five, yes. And here you had (inaudible) one of the top bands in the country, you know, the beginning, you know, like -- I guess Fletcher wasn't paying too much more money at the Roseland. Maybe seventy, a hundred, maybe a hundred -- the guys making (inaudible) or something like that. But that was like -- But you remember, the living conditions was down to nothing. You could take ten dollars then and go out and fill up your whole ice box for a week, a month, you know. Where could you buy for ten dollars a day? Nothing. You couldn't even -- you went in a
